name: HIPAA and Generative AI Tools
blurb: When chatbots can and cannot be used with patient data.
title: HIPAA and Generative AI Tools
answer: Consumer versions of chatbots cannot be used with protected health information, because the vendor will not sign a business associate agreement for them. Enterprise and API offerings can be covered by one, and AI vendors now sell healthcare editions built for that purpose.

reading.body:
The dividing line for generative AI in health care is the business associate agreement, not the model's quality. Consumer chatbot plans are not covered by one, so protected health information cannot go into them. Enterprise and API offerings can be covered, and vendors now sell healthcare editions built for that purpose.

The pattern is contractual rather than technical. The same underlying model can be unusable in its consumer form and usable in its enterprise form, because the vendor's willingness to sign a business associate agreement differs between the two. That makes procurement and vendor terms the gate on clinical use, ahead of any question about accuracy or capability.

For AI specifically, this matters because the tools clinicians most want to reach for are general purpose and widely available. A ban that stops at policy leaves staff without an approved path, which is why the guidance is to pair the ban with an alternative. The risk is not that the model is uniquely dangerous with patient data, it is that the covered entity has no agreement in place when something goes wrong.

What this does not cover is the substance of the agreements themselves, what they require of a vendor, or how enforcement works. It also says nothing about whether enterprise healthcare editions perform better on clinical tasks. The data establishes who may handle patient data and under what arrangement, not what the tools are good at.

The agreement is a vendor-by-vendor and product-by-product distinction, not a company-level one. OpenAI signs business associate agreements for eligible enterprise and API services and does not sign them for consumer ChatGPT plans, so the same firm sits on both sides of the line. A hospital cannot resolve the question by asking whether a vendor will sign, only by asking whether the specific service it intends to deploy is eligible.

That structure explains why the practical instruction is a ban paired with an approved alternative rather than a ban alone. If the only tool a clinician has is the consumer one, the policy forbids the work without providing a compliant way to do it, and the workaround is predictable. The approved path has to exist before the prohibition means anything.

The healthcare editions are the vendor's answer to that gap. OpenAI for Healthcare is sold to hospitals and health systems, which is a product decision made in response to the contractual constraint rather than a capability one. Nothing in the data says those editions are better at clinical tasks, only that they are the versions a covered entity can lawfully use.

Can a hospital use ChatGPT with patient data if it has an enterprise agreement?
Only if the specific service is one OpenAI covers. OpenAI states it signs business associate agreements for eligible enterprise and API services, and not for consumer ChatGPT plans.

Does OpenAI sign business associate agreements at all?
Yes, for eligible enterprise and API services. The consumer plans are excluded.

What is OpenAI for Healthcare?
A product OpenAI launched for hospitals and health systems. The data does not describe its features or how it differs from the enterprise offering.

Can a clinician paste de-identified notes into a consumer chatbot?
The data does not address de-identification or any category short of protected health information, so it cannot answer this.

What should a care team do instead of banning AI tools outright?
Ban consumer tools for patient data in policy and in practice, and give staff an approved alternative so they do not work around the ban.

Do the healthcare editions perform better on clinical tasks?
The data does not say. It establishes who may handle patient data and under what arrangement, not what the tools are good at.
